      <description>Britisk politi bekrefter overfor BBC at de har innledet en etterforskning mot komikeren David Walliams for alvorlige seksuelle forbrytelser.
Det skjer etter at flere kvinner har stått frem med anklager om at Walliams skal ha brukt kjendisstatusen sin for å tilnærme seg unge kvinner seksuelt.
Ifølge politiet er det ikke disse anklagene som er grunnlaget for etterforskningen.
Walliams er kjent for humorserien «Little Britain» og har de senere årene blant annet gjort seg bemerket som barnebokforfatter.
Han har avvist å ha gjort noe galt.</description>

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/thore-_henki_-holm-hansen-er-dod-1.18081252</link>
      <description>Den tidligere Outlaws-sjefen og countrymusikeren er død, 82 år gammel, melder VG.
Holm Hansen ledet MC-klubben Outlaws, ble dømt for handel med narkotika og våpen og ga ut countrymusikk.
«Han sovnet stille inn på morgenen i dag, hjemme hos meg i sin egen seng, med venner og familie rundt seg», skriver datteren hans June Nordlie i et innlegg på Facebook.
Holm Hansen ble i 1981 dømt til 60 års fengsel i en kokainsak i USA, men ble besluttet deportert til Norge.
Selv hevdet han at dommen var et justismord, og knyttet saken til påstått arbeid for CIA.</description>

      <description>Microsoft opplever tekniske problemer som rammer brukere av blant annet e-posttjenesten Outlook og Teams. Selskapet opplyser at de jobber med å løse saken.

      <description>En buss kjørte i dag tidlig av veien i Røn i Vestre Slidre.
Politiet opplyser at bussen skal ha sklidd av veien i lav hastighet, men at den ligger på siden.

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/skolebuss-av-veien-i-larvik-1.18079991</link>
      <description>Nødetatene har fått melding om en skolebuss som har kjørt av veien i Larvik.
– Bussen har sklidd av veien og ut i grøfta med alle fire hjul. I bussen er det 24 barn som fremstår uskadd, skriver operasjonsleder Per Magne Eftang i politiloggen.
Bussjåføren er også uskadd, ifølge politiet.
– Barna er nå på vei ut av bussen og inn et hus for å holde varmen, sier Eftang til NRK.
Han sier alle barna brukte bilbelte.
Operasjonslederen antar at hendelsen kan knyttes til det glatte føret, men politiet har ikke kommet fram til stedet ennå.
Klokka 09.44 opplyser politiet at ingen er skadet. Flere foreldre har hentet barna sine og ny buss er klar til å frakte resten av barna til skolen.</description>

    <item>
      <title>CNN: Demokratene vinner historisk senatsvalg i Mississippi</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/cnn_-demokratene-vinner-historisk-senatsvalg-i-mississippi-1.18079865</link>
      <description>Demokraten Scott Colom har vunnet senatsvalget i den tradisjonelt republikanske delstaten Mississippi, ifølge CNNs prognose.
Colom slår dermed den sittende republikanske senatoren Cindy Hyde-Smith, melder CNN onsdag kveld.
Han blir den første demokraten som representerer Mississippi i Senatet på over 40 år.
Colom blir også den første svarte politikeren som velges til et politisk verv av velgerne i hele Mississippi siden gjenoppbyggingsperioden etter den amerikanske borgerkrigen på 1800-tallet.
Valget ble holdt 3. november, men opptellingen har trukket ut i over en uke. Onsdag ettermiddag ledet Colom med rundt 3000 stemmer da om lag 98 prosent av stemmene var talt opp.
Resultatet er ennå ikke formelt godkjent. Fylkene i delstaten har frist til fredag med å godkjenne sine valgresultater.
(NTB)</description>

      <title>Norge gir 600 regnskogmillioner til Brasil</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/norge-gir-600-regnskogmillioner-til-brasil-1.18077109</link>
      <description>Klimaminister Sigrun Aasland (Ap) har med en stor sum når hun mandag reiser til åpningen av klimatoppmøtet i Tyrkia.
– Vi har med 600 millioner kroner til Brasil, for de har levert veldig gode resultater på å hindre avskoging i 2025, sier Aasland.
Brasil har det siste året redusert avskogningen til det laveste nivået siden målingene staret for over 40 år siden.
Gjennom den norske regnskogsatsingen gir Norge økonomisk støtte til Brasil når de klarer å redusere avskogingen.
– Norge finansierer resultater, og nå har vi med oss finansiering av de gode resultatene i Brasil, sier Aasland.</description>

Most of Vancouver Island remains under a rainfall warning, while another portion is under a coastal flooding statement on Friday.

The first big storm of the fall season continues to batter the west coast with a rainfall warning remaining in effect for Inland and West Vancouver Island.

Amounts of 50 to 100 mm of rain is expected, with some areas receiving 120 mm.

“The rain will ease late this afternoon,” Environment Canada says in a note in its Weather Information page.

“The highest rainfall amounts are anticipated near Zeballos and Tahsis and over the northern sections of Inland Vancouver Island, including Gold River.”

Though the rain will ease for the afternoon, it may only be for a brief period, with another weather system expected to bring more rain over the weekend.

“Water will likely pool on roads and in low-lying areas. Some travel delays are possible. Local utility outages are possible. Landslides may occur in vulnerable areas such as steep slopes, deforested areas or recent burn scars,” Environment Canada says.

“Watch for washouts near rivers, creeks and culverts.”

A coastal flooding statement is also in effect for Southern Gulf Islands, Saanich Inlet, Swartz Bay to Cordova Bay, Cordova Bay to East Sooke.

“A series of Pacific low-pressure systems will move across the region from now into the weekend and coincide with a period of high tides,” Environment Canada says.

“High tides are likely to surpass predicted levels due to storm surge enhancement.”

East to Southeasterly winds of 60-80 kilometres per hour are expected starting on Friday into the weekend over exposed coastal sections at times.

“Moderate to potentially strong winds accompanying these systems can also cause enhanced wave action and swells in some areas,” Environment Canada says.

RCMP say two people are dead and one person is missing after a boating tragedy in the Squamish Valley north of Vancouver, where a river is swollen by floodwaters and days of heavy rain.

Police say all others involved in the incident that happened on Thursday around 2 p.m. have been accounted for.

Cpl. Ashley MacKay with Squamish RCMP says search, rescue and recovery operations are continuing in the “time-sensitive and complex response.”

MacKay says in a statement that the search is challenging due to elevated water levels and weather conditions.

Squamish RCMP says the search involves Squamish Search and Rescue, RCMP Air Services, the Lower Mainland District Integrated Emergency Response Team, the RCMP Underwater Recovery Team, and West Coast Marine Services.

Legislator Jeremy Valeriote, who represents West Vancouver-Sea to Sky, says he’s “devastated” and his thoughts are with the families of the victims.

A very special birthday party is being held at the Courtenay and District Museum and Palaeontology Centre on Nov. 14.

It’s for the Puntledge River elasmosaur, Traskasaura sandrae, which will be turning 80,000,038 in the company of community members and cake.

Technically, the party is a celebration of the 38 years since the discovery of the 80 million-year-old elasmosaur fossil, but Courtenay Museum curator of natural history Pat Trask said it’s all about the fun.

“It’s a celebration of discovery,” he said. “I thought, well why don’t we have a birthday party for the day it was found?”

‘A catalyst’ for paleontology in the area

The Discourse has previously reported on these ancient marine reptiles which swam in the oceans of the late Cretaceous period, around 85-million years ago. The animals resembled the Loch Ness monster, with a small head and a neck as long as its bulbous body.

The specimen that is now at the Courtenay Museum was the first of its kind found west of the Canadian Rocky Mountains, and Trask describes it as a catalyst for paleontology on Vancouver Island.

“It was a spark that started a cascade of discoveries,” Trask said. “I mean, hundreds and hundreds of discoveries. Things that have never been seen before by science. New names, new creatures, unknown things.”

Trask’s late brother, Mike Trask, alongside his brother’s daughter, Heather Trask, discovered the fossil in November 1988. Pat Trask said although he’d always enjoyed looking for fossils as a kid in Ontario, his brother and niece’s discovery sparked an even greater passion.

RELATED: Dinosaur find near Cumberland could be second elasmosaur found by brothers

Pat Trask has now been collecting fossils and educating the public for 33 years.

“My job is to go fossil collecting just about every day, lead tours of classes of kids or the general public and teach them about the fossil record in the local area,” Trask said. “I love my job.”

In 1992, the Vancouver Island Paleontological Society was formed, sparked by the discovery of the elasmosaur. The society was the first of its kind in the province.

In October 2023, the elasmosaur was designated B.C.’s official fossil.

After Pat Trask found another elasmosaur specimen to join his brother’s, the new genus and species was officially scientifically named in 2025: Traskasaura Sandrae, with the Trask honouring Mike, Heather and Pat Trask.

F. Robin O’Keefe, an associate professor of biology from Marshall University in West Virginia, was the lead author of the scientific paper naming the elasmosaur. Pat Trask was among the co-authors of the paper.

It was both an exciting and sad time for Trask because his brother died eight days before the scientific paper officially naming the elasmosaur came out.

However, Trask did get to tell his brother the news beforehand.

Trask now sports a proud elasmosaur tattoo on his arm with its scientific name.

RELATED: Fierce-looking B.C. fossil confirmed as new genus, days after death of discoverer

Courtenay museum brings in worldwide researchers

Trask said the paper, as well as many of the other fossil discoveries around the Comox Valley, have drawn scholars to the area.

The museum has had visitors from the University of Tokyo to study the abundance of cephalopods in the area. They found a commonality to the fossils on Japan’s north island of Hokkaido.

“We have an open door policy. [A few] weeks ago we had a researcher from Warsaw, Poland,” he said. “He spent many hours with me going through one specific fossil in our collection.”

But to Trask, the elasmosaur is still a one-of-a-kind specimen because of what it represents.

“It represents the science of paleontology in the province of B.C.,” he said.

“That’s why it’s the provincial fossil. The same [provincial] status as the dogwood and the Western red-cedar.”

The museum has been hosting a birthday party since 2008, every Saturday after Remembrance Day.

This year, the party takes place from 11 a.m. until 2 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 14. Admission is by donation and the event is open to the public.

Trask said the whole place will be decorated like a giant birthday party with cake, crafts and balloons.

“It’s all about the fun and the sugar,” he said, adding that last year the turnout was about 300 people, but they have had 500 before.

“I expect [this year’s] to be big because it’s going to be rainy all week, the kids are going to want to get out of the house,” he said.

Trask said seeing children so excited to celebrate the elasmosaur is his favourite part of the birthday.

“And singing happy birthday to a skeleton,” he laughed, adding that everybody — including the elasmosaur — gets birthday hats.

Vancouver Island is prone to wild weather but the extremes are becoming more frequent. From record-breaking heat and wildfire threats to powerful storms and flooding, scientists warn that as the planet warms, the risks to our communities will only grow.  

On June 29, 2021, a heat dome settled over the province and the temperature in Lytton reached an extreme 49 degrees Celsius, the hottest ever recorded across B.C.

The next day, a devastating wildfire ripped through the town, destroying 90 per cent of all structures.

Five months later, a series of powerful atmospheric rivers unleashed record rainfall across B.C. and Vancouver Island, triggering catastrophic flooding, landslides and widespread destruction.

Watch the story below:

Loading the player...

Andrew Weaver, Professor Emeritus, School of Earth and Ocean Sciences University of Victoria said the weather is venturing into uncharted territory.

“We’ve got to start getting used to this. We are going to get much much warmer, and these El Niños are going to get much much stronger. And precipitation is going to get much, much bigger. And the climate is changing at a rate that is unparalleled in several million years. So it’s not a good situation,” Weaver said.

Atmospheric rivers have become part of B.C.’s weather system.

Charles Curry, climate scientist for Pacific Climate Impacts Consortium (PCIC) at the University of Victoria (UVic) said studies indicate the intensity of atmospheric rivers, and the amount of moisture they carry, is growing.

“The majority have found that the intensities, or the amount of rainfall that will come in any given atmospheric river by about mid-century, and then into the late century is projected to be larger than it has been in the past. So that’s an individual storm,” Curry said.

The BC Coroners Service found 619 people died as a direct result of the heat dome in 2021.
At least five people died as a direct result of flooding, and mudslides during 2021’s atmospheric rivers.

READ RELATED: B.C. government marks 5 years since heat dome killed hundreds

Two people died on Vancouver Island during the October 2024 atmospheric river when their vehicles were swept off the washed-out Bamfield Road.

“Interior BC wildfires are out of control. They are going to get far worse. The boreal forest is already slumping because of permafrost degradation, and beetle infestation. And there’s going to be wildfires in the boreal forest,” Weaver said.

Scientists agree that if global temperatures rise by two degrees Celsius by the end of the century, extreme weather events will become more frequent and intense.

The Supreme Court of Canada won’t hear an appeal challenging the application of British Columbia’s foreign buyer tax on a real estate purchase involving joint ownership by a Canadian citizen and a foreign national.

The B.C. Court of Appeal had previously dismissed an appeal brought by a couple who jointly bought an apartment in Richmond, B.C., putting 95 per cent in the Canadian woman’s name, and five per cent in the name of her foreign partner.

But the man had actually paid 40 per cent of the purchase price, with the woman explaining the disparity by saying it was a Chinese custom for a husband to pay a “bride price” by buying his wife a home. 

The couple, who were engaged in 2014 when they bought the home under a presale contract, paid the foreign buyer tax on only the five per cent registered to the foreign man, but an audit later found the tax “payable on the fair market value of the whole property.”

The B.C. government had told the lower court the rule was meant to “prevent tax avoidance by foreign investors who own beneficial interests held indirectly by others.”

The Supreme Court of Canada refused the couple leave to appeal on Thursday.

The couple had claimed imposing the tax on the entire value of the property was “profoundly unfair,” but the three-judge panel of the Appeal Court found they could have avoided paying the tax on the property’s entire value if they had registered ownership based on their contributions to the purchase price. 

The appellate ruling from earlier this year said the man, Li-Yuan Chuang, paid 40 per cent of the purchase price, but registered only a five per cent stake in the property, which the couple declared to have a value of $474,500 at the time of purchase.

His Canadian partner, Chia-Wen Hsia, said it was “customary in Chinese culture to pay for ‘bride price’ as in the husband buying a house for the wife.”

“In my husband’s case, he is not rich so he could only pay for part of the purchase price,” Hsia is quoted as saying in the appellate ruling. 

The B.C. Supreme Court initially dismissed the couple’s legal challenge in 2024.

The most recent assessed value for the two-bedroom apartment in the Avanti Richmond complex is $820,000.

The original B.C. Supreme Court ruling said a B.C. Finance Ministry tax analyst put the additional tax owed by the couple at just over $126,000. 

The B.C. foreign buyer tax is 20 per cent of market value.

The couple’s lawyer, Massao Morinaga, said they had no comment about the Supreme Court of Canada’s dismissal of the case.

He said it was the “end of the road judicially,” but the current foreign buyer tax legislation is drafted in a way that “captures situations that are inequitable.”

As the overtime ban for BC Transit workers in Victoria continues, the needed repairs for buses are piling up, with one-third of the fleet out of service, according to the union.

Unifor Local 333-BC’s overtime ban restarted on Oct. 5 after the union and company ended mediation without an agreement.

READ PREVIOUS: Victoria transit overtime ban coming back after mediation ends with no deal: ‘Not there yet’

More than one month later, Stephen Bains, president of the local, says the backlog of work is growing.

“Cancellations are averaging about 250 a day for the last couple weeks now,” Bains said.

Bains says on Thursday, there were 185 buses operating, but 222 are needed on the roads for a full service.

“So generally speaking, the overtime ban is starting to have impacts on the system, which is reliant on overtime,” he said.

Bains says the Victoria fleet has 320 buses, and on Thursday morning there were 125 in the queue waiting for repairs. Meaning rather than being out on the roads, they’re parked at a depot, which has frustrated the workers.

“Our members, who work with pride, they want to finish their jobs,” Bains said. “I hope the public realizes that we are fighting for transit schedules that suit their needs, and this overtime ban highlights how fragile the system is. Bains says the two parties are set to head back to the bargaining table on Friday, and have each continued meeting with the mediators to try and reach an agreement.

“Tomorrow will be the first time we’ve met face to face, and the union’s looking for a fair deal, and hopefully we get one,” he said.

BC Transit said to CHEK News that due to the interregnum period following the provincial election, the government remains in caretaker mode so it is unable to provide a comment.

Bains says some of the sticking points in bargaining remain wages and improved run and recovery times.

“We’re trying to do more with less, and that includes adding in runs without the actual funding of essentially transit hours that account for the human element, and so we’re finding ourselves in a situation where we’re now having to collectively bargain the human element,” he said.

“And that includes ensuring time for our operators to have a meal and use the washroom, and when that is successfully implemented into the schedule, the end result is a schedule that the passengers can rely on to run on time and get them to their destination on time.”
